# Graph Quasirandomness for Hypothesis Testing of Stochastic Block Models

**Authors:** Kiril Bangachev ††thanks: Dept. of EECS, MIT. kirilb@mit.edu Guy Bresler ††thanks: Dept. of EECS, MIT. guy@mit.edu. Supported by NSF Grant CCF-2428619.

## Abstract

The celebrated theorem of Chung, Graham, and Wilson on quasirandom graphs implies that if the 4-cycle and edge counts in a graph $G$ are both close to their typical number in $\mathbb{G}(n,1/2),$ then this also holds for the counts of subgraphs isomorphic to $H$ for any $H$ of constant size. We aim to prove a similar statement where the notion of close is whether the given (signed) subgraph count can be used as a test between $\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)$ and a stochastic block model $\mathbb{SBM}.$

Quantitatively, this is related to approximately maximizing $H\longrightarrow|\Phi(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}},$ where $\Phi(H)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $\mathbb{SBM}$ , indexed by subgraph $H.$ This formulation turns out to be equivalent to approximately maximizing the partition function of a spin model over alphabet equal to the community labels in $\mathbb{SBM}.$

We resolve the approximate maximization when $\mathbb{SBM}$ satisfies one of four conditions: 1) the probability of an edge between any two vertices in different communities is exactly $1/2$ ; 2) the probability of an edge between two vertices from any two communities is at least $1/2$ (this case is also covered in a recent work of Yu, Zadik, and Zhang); 3) the probability of belonging to any given community is at least $c$ for some universal constant $c>0$ ; 4) $\mathbb{SBM}$ has two communities. In each of these cases, we show that there is an approximate maximizer of $|\Phi(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}$ in $\mathcal{A}=\{\text{stars, 4-cycle}\}.$ This implies that if there exists a constant-degree polynomial test distinguishing $\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)$ and $\mathbb{SBM},$ then the two distributions can also be distinguished via the signed count of some graph in $\mathcal{A}.$ We conjecture that the same holds true for distinguishing $\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)$ and any graphon if we also add triangles to $\mathcal{A}.$

Keywords: Stochastic Block Models, Quasirandom Graphs, Low Degree Polynomial Tests.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Background

#### Quasirandomness.

In the seminal paper [CGW88], Chung, Graham, and Wilson initiated the study of quasirandom graphs. The central question addressed by quasirandomness is:

Does the graph $G$ resemble a random graph?

[CGW88] establishes the equivalence of several seemingly disparate properties that make a graph similar to a sample from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ or, in their terminology, quasirandom. To describe the result, we denote by $\mathsf{C}_{H}(G)$ the number of labeled copies of $H$ in a graph $G$ (so, for example, $\mathsf{C}_{H}(\mathsf{K}_{n})=n(n-1)\cdots(n-|\mathsf{V}(H)|+1)$ for any $H$ ) and by $\mathsf{C}^{*}_{H}(G)$ the number of induced labeled copies.

#### Theorem 1.1 ([CGW88]).

The following conditions are equivalent for an $n$ -vertex graph $G:$

- P1) $|\mathsf{C}^{*}_{H}(G)|=(1+o(1))n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}2^{-\binom{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}{2}},$ which is equivalent to $|\mathsf{C}_{H}(G)|=(1+o(1))n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}2^{-|\mathsf{E}(H)|},$ for all graphs $H$ of constant size.

- P2) $|\mathsf{E}(G)|\geq(1+o(1))\frac{n^{2}}{4}$ and $|\mathsf{C}_{\mathsf{Cyc}_{t}}(G)|\leq\frac{n^{t}}{2^{t}}(1+o(1))$ for some cycle $\mathsf{Cyc}_{t}$ of even length $t\geq 4.$

- P3) $|\mathsf{E}(G)|\geq(1+o(1))\frac{n^{2}}{4}$ and $\lambda_{1}(G)=\frac{n}{2}(1+o(1)),\lambda_{2}(G)=o(n)$ where these are the largest two eigenvalues of $G$ by absolute value.

- P4) For each subset $S$ of $\mathsf{V}(H),$ the number of edges restricted to this subset is $\frac{|S|^{2}}{4}+o(|\mathsf{V}(H)|^{2}).$

- P5) For each subset $S$ of $\mathsf{V}(H)$ with $S=\lfloor n/2\rfloor,$ the number of edges restricted to this subset is $(1+o(1))\frac{n^{4}}{16}.$

- P6) $\displaystyle\sum_{v\neq v^{\prime}\in\mathsf{V}(H)}\bigg|\sum_{u\in\mathsf{V}(H)}\mathds{1}[G_{vu}=G_{v^{\prime}u}]-n/2\bigg|=o(n^{3}).$

- P7) $\displaystyle\sum_{v\neq v^{\prime}\in\mathsf{V}(H)}\bigg|\sum_{u\in\mathsf{V}(H)}\mathds{1}[G_{vu}=G_{v^{\prime}u}=1]-n/4\bigg|=o(n^{3}).$

In particular, if $G$ has a number of 4-cycles and edges close to that of a typical sample from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)},$ then any other subgraph count as well as the spectrum of $G$ resemble that of Erdős-Rényi.

#### Hypothesis Testing for Graph Structure.

Subgraph counts and spectral statistics are commonly used to compare random graphs to Erdős-Rényi in a different framework – when testing for hidden structure in random graph distributions. Concretely, the following hypothesis testing question has received considerable attention from the probability, computer science, and theoretical statistics communities. For a family of distributions $(\mathbb{P}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ over $n$ -vertex graphs, one aims to solve the following hypothesis testing problem on input an $n$ -vertex graph $G$ :

$$ \mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}\quad\text{ versus }\quad\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}. $$

Both the information-theoretic question (is there a consistent test?) and the computational question (is there a computationally-efficient test?) are active research areas for many choices of $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ in (HT).

Popular choices of $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ in (HT) include graph distributions with the following types of hidden structure: Community structure such as stochastic block models [HLL83, BCLS84, DF89, Bop87, BJR07, RL08, CO10, DKMZ11, Mas14, MNS18] (and many more in [Abb18]), in particular the planted clique [Kuč95, Jer92, AKS98, BHK+19, BBH18, BB19, BB20, HS24]; Geometric structure such as random geometric graphs [DGLU11, BDER14, BBN19, BBH24, LR23a, LMSY22, LR23b, FGKS24, BB24a, BB24b, BB25]; Planted dense subgraph such as a matching, clique, or cycle [HWX15, DWXY21, MNWS+23, DMW25, YZZ24] (in addition to planted clique references).

One natural and computationally efficient approach to (HT) is to compare simple statistics of $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}.$ For example, if $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ has a lot more triangles than ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ (as in the case of random geometric graphs over the sphere, see [BDER14]), then one can use this fact to distinguish the two distributions. The semblance with the classic quasirandomness theory, initiated in Theorem 1.1, is striking – subgraph counts are used to compare with Erdős-Rényi.

#### Towards a Quasirandomness Theory for Hypothesis Testing for Graph Structure.

In the context of (HT), the question of graph quasirandomness takes the following form:

Is there a small set of simple graph statistics such that if $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ are indistinguishable under these statistics, then they are also computationally / information-theoretically indistinguishable?

Of course, one may speculate that Theorem 1.1 already answers this question. If the 4-cycle count and edge count of $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ are sufficiently close, then so are all other subgraph counts. Hence, polynomials in the edges of the two graph distributions are also close. Within the increasingly popular framework of low-degree polynomial tests (see Section 2.2 for definitions), this would give evidence for computational indistinguishability.

The reason this argument fails is that Theorem 1.1 is quantitatively too weak in the $o(1)$ dependence on the number of vertices. For example, consider $\mathbb{P}_{n}=\mathbb{G}(n,1/2+1/\sqrt{n}).$ According to Theorem 1.1, (a sample from) this graph distribution is quasirandom. However, one can easily distinguish $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ : A simple concentration argument shows that with high probability, the first distribution has more than $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}+\frac{1}{8}n^{1.5}$ edges, while the second less than $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}+\frac{1}{8}n^{1.5}.$ In Section 1.5.2, we explain why even careful book-keeping of the $o(1)$ -dependencies in Theorem 1.1 is not sufficient. There is a fundamental barrier to the techniques used for Theorem 1.1 and a different approach is needed to develop a quasirandomness theory in the setting of hypothesis testing.

In the recent work [YZZ24], the authors make a first step towards this end.11 1 To the best of our knowledge, the connection of their work to graph quasirandomness was not known to the authors of [YZZ24].

#### Theorem 1.2 ([YZZ24]).

Let $(H_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of fixed $n$ -vertex graphs. The sequence of planted distributions $\mathbb{P}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ over $n$ -vertex graphs is defined as follows. To sample from $\mathbb{P}_{n},$ one first samples $\mathbf{G}$ from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)},$ 22 2 The results of [YZZ24] and the current work extend appropriately for any ${\mathbb{G}(n,q)}$ when $q\in(0,1)$ is an absolute constant (independent on $n$ ). We choose to work with $q=1/2$ as this makes nearly no difference in the arguments. We do note that if we allow $q$ to depend on $n,$ we expect the behavior to change dramatically, see Section 5. then adds the edges of $H_{n},$ producing $\mathbf{G}\cup H_{n},$ and finally applies a uniformly random permutation to the vertices of $\mathbf{G}\cup H_{n}.$

There exists a constant degree polynomial test that distinguishes $\mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}$ with high probability if and only if there exists some signed star count that distinguishes $\mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}$ with high probability.

We will explain the precise meaning of constant degree polynomial test and signed subgraph count in a moment. More important for now is the interpretation of the theorem from a quasirandomness perspective: if signed star counts between $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ are sufficiently similar, then so are also all other constant-degree polynomial statistics.

The goal of this work is to extend the above theorem to a more diverse family of distributions. Specifically, the choice of model in Theorem 1.2 makes the following strong structural assumption: Even conditioned on the latent planted graph $H,$ the edge $\mathbf{G}_{ij}$ has marginal probability of appearance at least $1/2$ . Both the methods and conclusion of Theorem 1.2 break down in some of the simplest models that do not exhibit this structure. For example, the following distribution is easily distinguishable from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ via counting signed 4-cycles but signed stars fail to distinguish it. Each of $n$ vertices receives an independent uniformly random label $1$ or 2. If $u$ and $v$ receive the same label, they are adjacent with probability $1/2+n^{-1/10}.$ If $u$ and $v$ receive different labels, they are adjacent with probability $1/2-n^{-1/10}.$ One can show that the expected number of signed stars is the same as in ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ : zero. The reason is that even conditioned on the latent label of $u,$ the edge $\mathbf{G}_{u,v}$ is distributed as $\mathsf{Bern}(1/2),$ due to the randomness of the label of $v.$

#### Our Conjecture and Results.

We make the following quasirandomness conjecture for hypothesis testing of a stochastic block model (Definition 1 below) against Erdős-Rényi.

#### Conjecture 1.

Suppose that $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is a stochastic block model (whose parameters may depend arbitrarily on $n$ ) which one aims to distinguish from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}.$ There exists a constant degree polynomial test that distinguishes $\mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}$ with high probability if and only if one of the following signed subgraph counts

$$ \{\textsf{edge, stars, triangle, 4-cycle}\} $$

distinguishes $\mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}$ with high probability.

We note that [YZZ24] implicitly proves the conjecture whenever, even conditioned on the labels, any two vertices have a probability of connection at least $1/2.$

Our main contribution is to prove this conjecture in the following additional cases:

- 1. $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is an arbitrary stochastic block model on 2 communities.

- 2. $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is an arbitrary stochastic block model on a constant number of communities and each community label appears with constant positive probability.

- 3. $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is a stochastic block model in which every two vertices in distinct communities are adjacent with probability $1/2.$

The stochastic block model is of special interest for several reasons. First, it is perhaps the most widely studied family of random graph distributions after Erdős-Rényi. Second, as we will see in the forthcoming section, the above results for stochastic block models with $k$ -communities can be equivalently phrased as an approximate maximization of the partition function of a certain spin-glass model with alphabet of size $k.$ The interaction matrix of the spin model is determined by the stochastic block model interaction matrix and external fields correspond to the community probabilities. This gives an alternative statistical-mechanics interpretation of our results in addition to the quasirandomness perspective. Finally, stochastic block models can approximate arbitrarily well smooth graphons. In fact, we believe that Conjecture 1 should hold more generally for graphons.

### 1.2 Implications and Interpretations of Conjecture 1

#### Fine-Grained Running Times.

A degree- $D$ polynomial in the edges of an $n$ -vertex graph may take up to time $n^{2D}$ to compute and, hence, be completely impractical. Yet, Conjecture 1 tells us that we only need to compute signed star counts or signed 3- and 4-cycle counts. Signed counts of stars can be computed in near-linear time as the signed star count with a fixed central vertex $v$ is a simple one-dimensional functional of the degree of the vertex (which can trivially be computed in time $O(D)$ where $D$ is the star size). One simply needs to evaluate and add this function over all possible central vertices. On the other hand, signed triangles and 4-cycle counts can be evaluated in $n^{\omega}$ time, where $\omega\in[2,2.371\ldots]$ is the matrix-multiplication time [WXXZ24]. Indeed, the signed triangle count of a graph with adjacency matrix $A$ is is $\mathsf{trace}((2A-11^{T})^{3})$ and the signed 4-cycle count is $\mathsf{trace}((2A-11^{T})^{4})-n(n-1)(2n-3).$ Hence, if there exists a constant-degree polynomial distinguisher, there also exists a practical one.

More succinctly, our result suggests a strong dichotomy for the complexity of testing stochastic block-models with low-degree polynomial tests. Either there exists a low-degree distinguisher implementable in nearly-quadratic time or there does not exist any constant-degree polynomial distinguisher.

#### On Finding A Distinguisher.

The practical distinguisher is easy to find as noted in [YZZ24] – it is a signed star, triangle, or 4-cycle count. Hence, a statistician in practice may also simply try each of these tests. They do not even need to know the specific parameters of the stochastic block model, but only the fact that it is part of a family satisfying Conjecture 1.

Conversely, the failure of a very small set of tests (the signed counts of triangles, 4-cycles, starts) implies the failure of ALL low-degree polynomial tests.

#### Our Conjecture And Results in The Context of Low-Degree Hardness.

The current work and [YZZ24] are preceded by a long line of low-degree polynomial hardness results on testing between Erdős-Rényi and random graph models [BHK+19, HS17a, Hop18, BB25, BB24a, BB24b, MWZ23, MWZ24, KVWX23, RSWY23, MVW24] (nearly all of which are graphons).. We remark that there is an important conceptual difference between these prior results and ours. Our work does not prove hardness for any specific model (and in fact does not prove explicitly any hardness result). Instead, our work and [YZZ24] aim to derive certain universality principles for the low-degree polynomial framework itself over a rich family of testing problems. In this light, our work more closely resembles the universal (near)-equivalence between low-degree polynomial tests and SQ algorithms in [BBH+21].

### 1.3 Signed Subgraph Counts, Stochastic Block Models, and Partition Functions

We now introduce the main ingredients necessary to describe our results.

#### Signed Subgraph Counts.

To derive a quantitatively stronger form of Theorem 1.1, we need to quantify what it means for a subgraph count to be different enough from that of Erdős-Rényi so that one can use it towards (HT). We borrow the notion from the framework of low-degree polynomial tests [HS17a, Hop18] as in [YZZ24]. Let $H$ be a graph. On input an $n$ -vertex graph $G,$ compute the signed count of $H$ ,

$$ \mathsf{SC}_{H}(G)\coloneqq\sum_{H_{1}\sim H}\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2G_{ij}-1)\,, $$

where the sum is over all isomorphic copies of $H_{1}$ in the complete graph $\mathsf{K}_{n}$ and $G_{ij}$ is the indicator of the respective edge. Compare with the unsigned count $\mathsf{C}_{H}(G)$ from Theorem 1.1, which corresponds to $\mathsf{C}_{H}(G)\coloneqq\sum_{H_{1}\sim H}\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}G_{ij}.$ The advantage of working with signed counts in the hypothesis testing setting is that they have a smaller variance (as noted by [BDER14]) with respect to ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ due to the fact that the signs of different subgraphs are uncorrelated (see Theorem 2.1).

One condition that would guarantee that $\mathsf{SC}_{H}$ distinguishes $\mathsf{H}_{0}:{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}:\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{1}}\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})-\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{0}}\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})\Big|=\omega\Big(\max\Big(\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{0}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2},\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{1}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2}\Big)\Big). $$

If (2) holds, one can test between $\mathsf{H}_{1}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{0}$ by evaluating $\mathsf{SC}_{H}$ on the input $G.$ If $G\sim\mathsf{H}_{b}$ for $b\in\{0,1\},$ then $\displaystyle\mathsf{SC}_{H}(G)\in[\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{b}}\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})\pm C\times\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{H}_{b}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2}]\eqqcolon I_{b}$ with high probability for large enough $C=\omega(1)$ by Chebyshev’s inequality. Condition (2) ensures that $I_{0},I_{1}$ are disjoint for some appropriate $C$ and, hence, one can test by reporting the membership of $\mathsf{SC}_{H}$ to one of $I_{0},I_{1}.$

Under the ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ distribution, when $H$ has a constant number of edges, it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]=0\quad\text{ and }\quad\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]=\sum_{H_{1}\sim H}1=\Theta(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}). $$

Thus, one can rephrase (2) as $|\displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})|=\omega\Big(\max\big(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2},\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2}\big)\Big).$

If the distribution $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ is permutation invariant, that is any vertex permutation $\pi$ is measure-preserving with respect to $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ , one can further observe that

$$ \displaystyle\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}\mathsf{SC}_{H}(\mathbf{G})=\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2G_{ij}-1)\times\Bigg(\sum_{H_{1}\sim H}1\Bigg)=\Theta\Bigg(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}\Bigg[\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2G_{ij}-1)\Bigg]\Bigg). $$

The quantity

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\coloneqq\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}\Bigg[\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2G_{ij}-1)\Bigg] $$

denotes the Fourier coefficient of the distribution (i.e., of the probability mass function of) $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ corresponding to shape $H.$ Going back to (2), the inequality becomes

$$ n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)|=\omega(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2})\Longleftrightarrow|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}n^{1/2}=\omega(1). $$

Leaving aside the fact that (5) does not capture the variance under $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ 33 3 In our setting, it turns out that (5) can “nearly” capture the variance under $\mathbb{P}_{n}.$ We return to this in Theorem 2.4. , (5) suggests that the “most powerful” signed subgraph counts for distinguishing ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ are the (approximate) maximizers of

$$ H\longrightarrow\Psi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H),\text{ where }\Psi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\coloneqq|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}. $$

This motivates the following problem:

#### Problem 1 (Approximate Maximization of Scaled Fourier Coefficients / Approximate Maximization of SBM Partition Function).

For every $n\in\mathbb{N},$ let $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ be a family of random graph distributions over $n$ -vertex graphs invariant under vertex permutations. Let $\mathcal{F}=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{n}.$ Let $D\in\mathbb{N}$ be some fixed constant. Find some minimal set $\mathcal{A}_{D}$ of graphs on at most $D$ edges with the following property. There exists some constant $C_{D,\mathcal{F}}>0$ (depending only on $\mathcal{F},D$ ) such that for any graph $H$ without isolated vertices on at most $D$ edges and any $\mathbb{F}\in\mathcal{F},$

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\mathbb{F}}(H)\leq C_{D,\mathcal{F}}\times\max_{K\in\mathcal{A}_{D}}\Psi_{\mathbb{F}}(K). $$

To gain intuition about Problem 1, consider the setting of dense planted subgraphs of [YZZ24]. The authors implicitly show that the set of stars on at most $D$ edges is such a set $\mathcal{A}_{D}$ .

#### Stochastic Block Models.

One of the motivations of our work is to extend the results of [YZZ24] to a setting when, conditioned on the latent structure of the model, some of the edges might have a probability of appearance less than half. Stochastic block models are a canonical example.

#### Definition 1.

A stochastic block model on $k$ communities is parametrized by a probability vector $p=(p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{k})\in(0,1]^{k}$ and a symmetric matrix $Q\in[-1,1]^{k}.$ To generate an $n$ -vertex sample from $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q),$ one performs the following two-step process:

- 1. First, draw $n$ independent labels $\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}$ from the distribution over $[k]$ specified by $p.$

- 2. Produce an $n$ -vertex graph $\mathbf{G}$ by drawing each edge $(i,j)$ as an independent $\mathsf{Bern}(\frac{1+Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}}}{2})$ random variable.

More commonly, the SBM is defined with the probability matrix $M\in[0,1]^{k\times k}$ where $M_{i,j}=(1+Q_{i,j})/2,$ but the current parametrization is more convenient for discussing Fourier coefficients. We proceed with some examples:

- 1. Suppose that $Q=\mathbf{0}_{k\times k}$ is the zero matrix. Then, regardless of labels, each edge $(i,j)$ appears with probability $1/2.$ Hence, this is ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}.$

- 2. Suppose that $k=2,$ $p=(1/n^{\alpha},1-1/n^{\alpha})$ and $Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}.$ Then, $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ is the planted clique distribution with expected clique of size $n^{1-\alpha}.$ Namely, the vertices with label 1 form a clique and every other edge appears with probability $1/2.$

#### Partition Functions.

We now record an explicit formula for $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H).$ We will often write $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ instead of $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ whenever the dependence on $n$ is clear or unimportant. We write $\mathbf{x}\sim p$ for a variable distributed over $[k]$ with p.m.f. $p.$

#### Proposition 1.3.

Consider some $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ distribution and let $H$ be a graph on $h$ vertices. Then,

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\E_{(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{i=1}^{h}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}p}\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}}\Bigg]=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Big). $$

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that the vertices of $H$ are $\{1,2,\ldots,h\}.$ By definition,

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H) \displaystyle=\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Bigg|(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq h}\Bigg]\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}\E\Bigg[(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Bigg|(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq h}\Bigg]\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}\E\Bigg[(2\frac{1+Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}}}{2}-1)\Bigg|(\mathbf{x}_{i})_{1\leq i\leq h}\Bigg]\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}}\Bigg]=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg).\qed $$

The right hand-side would be the partition function of a $k$ -spin system if the matrix $Q$ had non-negative entries. Denoting $f(s)\coloneqq\log p_{s},g(s,t)\coloneqq\log Q_{s,t},$ we obtain the more familiar from spin systems expression

$$ \begin{split}\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}(H)&=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg)\\
&=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\exp\Bigg(\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}g(x_{i},x_{j})+\sum_{i\in\mathsf{V}(H)}f(x_{i})\Bigg)\eqqcolon Z_{H}(g,f).\end{split} $$

Hence, (approximately) maximizing $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}$ over graphs $H$ is the same as approximately maximizing $|Z_{H}(g,f)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}$ or, equivalently, $\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\log|Z_{H}(g,f)|.$ This problem has received a lot of attention for spin systems, most notably in the case of the hard-core model [Alo91, Kah01, Zha09, Gal11, DJPR17, SSSZ18, SSSZ19]. Yet, our task differs from prior work in at least two notable ways. What makes our problem easier is that we are content with approximate maximization of $|Z_{H}(g,f)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}$ (up to constant multiplicative factors) as this does not change the asymptotics of testing. What makes our problem harder is that the interaction terms $Q_{i,j}$ might be negative, so prior techniques, for example based on the bipartite swapping trick [Zha09], fail.

### 1.4 Our Results

#### 1.4.1 Results for Restricted Stochastic Block Models

#### Theorem 1.4 (Main Results on Testing and Partition Function Maximization).

Consider the $k$ -community stochastic block model $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q).$ Let $D$ be an even integer constant greater than $4.$ Then, in Problem 1,one can take the set $\mathcal{A}_{D}$ of approximate maximizers, to be:

- 1. Diagonal SBMs (Theorem 3.1): If $Q$ satisfies that $Q_{i,j}=0$ whenever $i\neq j,$ then one can take

$$ \mathcal{A}^{1}_{D}=\{\text{edge, star on 2 edges}\}. $$

- 2. Non-Negative SBMs (Theorem 3.3 and [YZZ24]): If $Q$ satisfies that $Q_{i,j}\geq 0$ for each $i,j,$ then one can take

$$ \mathcal{A}^{2}_{D}=\{\text{stars on at most $D$ edges}\}. $$

- 3. SBMs with Non-Vanishing Community Probabilities (Theorem 3.4): If $p$ satisfies that $p_{i}\geq c\;\forall i\in[k]$ for some universal constant $c,$ then one can take

$$ \mathcal{A}^{3}_{D}=\{\text{edge, star on 2 edges, 4-cycle}\}. $$

- 4. SBMs with Two Communities (Theorem 3.6): If $k=2$ and $D$ is even, then one can take

$$ \mathcal{A}^{4}_{D}=\{\text{stars on at most $D$ edges}\}\cup\{\text{4-cycles\lx@text@rbrace}. $$

Furthermore, in each of the cases above, if there is a constant degree polynomial test distinguishing the respective SBM model from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ with high probability, then one can also distinguish with high probability using the signed count of some graph in the respective $\mathcal{A}_{D}.$

We remark that allowing for small increase in the vertex size, the same theorem holds for degrees as large as $D=o(\log n/\log\log n).$ We formalize this in Proposition 5.1. We choose to write all the proofs for constant degree polynomials, $D=O(1)$ for simplicity of exposition, but the extensions to $D=o(\log n/\log\log n)$ are only a matter of careful bookkeeping. We do not pursue this direction since we are not aware of any concrete advantages of degree $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ polynomials over constant-degree polynomials. Different would have been the case if our techniques also captured degree $O(\log n)$ polynomials which encompass many spectral methods. This, however, seems challenging at present.

#### 1.4.2 One-to-one comparisons of Fourier coefficients: Results and Barriers

#### Barrier to one-to-one comparisons.

One natural approach to identifying such optimal sets $\mathcal{A}_{D}$ is via one-to-one comparisons of Fourier coefficients. For example in the case of diagonal SBMs, prove that for any $H,$ there exists some $\mathsf{K}\in\{\text{edge, wedge}\}$ such that $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)$ for any diagonal SBM. This indeed works for diagonal SBMs.

This simple approach, however, fails in the case of SBMs with non-vanishing community fractions and 2-SBMs (as demonstrated in Theorem A.8). Instead, we rely on many-to-one comparisons. For example in the case of 2-SBMs, we prove that for any $H$ and any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q),$ there exists some $\mathsf{K}_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}\in\{\text{stars on at most $D$ edges}\}\cup\{\text{4-cycles}\}$ such that

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\lesssim\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}). $$

The only difference from one-to-one comparison is in the order of quantifiers – here $\mathsf{K}$ can depend on the specific stochastic block model. This flexibility turns out to be necessary for results 3 and 4 in our Theorem 1.4 as demonstrated by Theorem A.8.

#### Some one-to-one comparisons.

It is still useful to consider what one-to-one comparisons we can obtain. We summarize below.

#### Theorem 1.5 (One-to-one comparison of Fourier Coefficients).

Consider any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q).$ Then:

- 1. Theorem 4.1: For any $t\geq 5,$ $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{t})\leq\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}).$

- 2. Theorem 4.3: If $H$ has a degree $d$ vertex, then $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})|^{1/2}.$

- 3. Theorem 4.2: Let $\mathsf{K}_{4}^{-}$ be the graph on 4 vertices with 5 edges. Then, $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{4}^{-})\leq\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}).$

The first statement explains why the only signed cycle counts for distinguishing stochastic block models and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ that appear in the literature are triangles (for example, planted coloring in [KVWX23]) and 4-cycles (for example, the quiet planting in [KVWX23]), but no larger cycle counts. The proof is a simple spectral argument, at a high-level, similar to the way spectrum (P3) and cycle counts (P2) in Theorem 1.1 are related in classical quasirandomness [CGW88, F4 and F5].

The second inequality also follows the proof of equivalence used in [CGW88, F12], namely used to show that (P6) implies (P1) in Theorem 1.1 (and, implicitly, appears in [LR23a] for our setting of signed subgraph counts). And while the quantitative dependence in the second inequality is strong enough to imply Theorem 1.1, it is too weak for the purposes of hypothesis testing. We would like to show the much stronger inequality $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})|^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})|}$ (note that $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})|\leq 1$ and $|\mathsf{V}(H)|\geq d+1\geq|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})|/2=(d+2)/2$ ).

Nevertheless, it turns out that in certain cases, one can improve the argument in Item 2 above. For example, Item 2 implies that $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{4}^{-})|\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{2,2})|^{1/2}.$ However, we show that in this specific case, the argument can be appropriately modified to imply the stronger, and sufficient for the hypothesis testing setting, inequality from Item 3: $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{4}^{-})|\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{K}_{2,2})|.$ This inequality also appears implicitly in [LR23a]. In particular, this result demonstrates why no examples in the literature appear in which one tests via signed $\mathsf{K}_{4}^{-}$ -counts.

#### 1.4.3 A Library of Examples

In Appendix A we provide example SBM distributions which demonstrate the necessity of different subgraph (signed) counts appearing in the respective sets $\mathcal{A}_{D}$ in Theorem 1.4. In Theorem A.2, we show that for certain SBMs even on just 2 balanced communities, one needs to go beyond the signed star counts proposed by [YZZ24] to distinguish the model from Erdős-Rényi with a constant-degree polynomial. In Theorem A.8, we illustrate the aforementioned necessity of many-to-one comparisons. Finally, with Theorems A.6, A.7, A.3, A.4 and A.5 we show that each of the triangle, 4-cycle, edge, wedge, and a large star necessarily belongs to the set in Conjecture 1.

### 1.5 Prior Techniques and Barriers

Our two main results are parts 3 and 4 of Theorem 1.4. We begin with an overview of previous techniques appearing in the recent work on planted graph models [YZZ24] and the classical quasirandomness theory [CGW88] and outline two barriers which prevent those techniques from working in our setting. Then, we explain our two new key ideas towards overcoming these barriers.

#### 1.5.1 Signed Stars in Planted-Subgraph Models

We begin with the recent work [YZZ24]. Adapted to our setting of stochastic block models, one part of their argument shows that if $Q_{i,j}\geq 0$ for all $i,j$ , then for any graph $H$ on at most $D$ edges without isolated vertices, there exists some star on $t\leq D$ edges such that $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{t}).$ For completeness, we give a full proof of this fact in Theorem 3.3, but here is a sketch of the proof. Recall (7) – for any graph $H$ without isolated vertices,

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Big). $$

Since all values of $Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}$ are non-negative and $[0,1]$ -valued, removing an edge from $H$ cannot decrease the quantity on the right hand-side. Hence, one can iteratively remove edges from $H.$ The only condition one needs to ensure is that there are no isolated vertices. Therefore, the process will terminate with a graph $K$ in which every connected component is a star. Stars are the only connected graphs from which one cannot remove an edge without creating isolated vertices. Altogether, this means that $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)$ where $K$ has $|\mathsf{V}(H)|$ vertices and every connected component is a star. An elementary factorization of Fourier coefficients of SBMs over connected components (Proposition 2.2) implies that $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{t})$ for some star graph on at most $D$ edges (one of the components of $K$ ).

The challenge of extending this argument to general $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ distributions when $Q$ has negative entries is that removing an edge can decrease the Fourier coefficient of a graph. This is illustrated in our Theorem A.2. Namely, take $k=2,p=(1/2,1/2)$ and $Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\ -1&1\end{pmatrix}.$ Let $H=\mathsf{K}_{4,4},$ the complete bipartite graph with two parts of size 4. One can show that $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=1$ (as $H$ has only even-degree vertices). However, for any edge $e,$ if $H\backslash e$ is the graph $H$ with edge $e$ deleted, $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H\backslash e)=0$ (as $H$ has an odd-degree vertex). Hence, removing an edge can dramatically decrease a Fourier coefficient – from being 1 and sufficient to test against ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ to being 0 and, thus, being completely useless towards distinguishing from ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}.$

The fact that edge-removals fail when $Q$ has negative entries is a serious obstacle towards proving our results 3 and 4 in Theorem 1.4. The reason is that we always want to compare the Fourier coefficient of a graph $H$ to the Fourier coefficient of very sparse graphs – stars or 4-cycle.

#### Challenge 1.

The natural approach of comparing the Fourier coefficient of a graph $H$ to a sparser graph by iteratively removing edges sometimes fails when $Q$ has negative entries, even on two communities each appearing with probability $1/2.$

Insight from Challenge 1: We need one-shot comparisons instead of iterative comparisons.

#### 1.5.2 Classical Quasirandomness

The celebrated Theorem 1.1 of [CGW88] gives several equivalent conditions for when the subgraph counts of graphs resemble that of Erdős-Rényi. One way to rewrite their results to make them more similar to our setting is as follows. Let $G$ be any graph on $n$ vertices and let $\mathbf{G}$ be $G$ after a uniformly random vertex permutation. Then, the condition $|\mathsf{C}_{H}(G)|=(1+o(1))n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}2^{-|\mathsf{E}(H)|}$ can be equivalently rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E\Big[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}\mathbf{G}_{i,j}\Big]-2^{-|\mathsf{E}(H)|}\Big|=o(1). $$

There are several ways in which (9) differs with our result:

- 1. Distributional: The distribution of $\mathbf{G}$ is not a stochastic block model. However, the stochastic block models is a vertex-symmetric distribution. In particular, Theorem 1.1 applies to (a high-probability sample of) the SBM distributions.

- 2. Signed versus Unsigned Counts: Theorem 1.1 is for unsigned counts $|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-2^{-|\mathsf{E}(H)|}|$ instead of signed counts $|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)|.$ This difference is again minor. Expanding the product in $\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)$ and applying triangle inequality shows that for constant size graphs $H,$ (9) is equivalent to $\displaystyle\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Big|=o(1).$ (10)

- 3. Scaling: The real problem with the approach of [CGW88] is the scaling. In place of (10), we need the much more fine-grained inequality (5): $|\E[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)]|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=o(n^{-1/2}).$ It turns out that improving (10) is not simply a matter of carefully keeping track of the $o(1)$ -dependence in [CGW88] as their methods are fundamentally too weak for our purposes. For example, an intermediate step in their argument (Fact 12), rewritten in the setting of Fourier coefficients of stochastic block models (see Theorem 1.5) gives that for any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ distribution, and graph $H$ with a degree $d$ vertex, $\displaystyle\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Big|\leq\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in E(\mathsf{K}_{2,d})}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1))\Big|^{1/2}.$ (11) So, take for example $H=\mathsf{K}_{4,4}.$ This inequality implies that if $\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in E(\mathsf{K}_{2,4})}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1))\Big|=o(1),$ then $\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(\mathsf{K}_{4,4})}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Big|=o(1).$ However, if $\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in E(\mathsf{K}_{2,4})}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1))\Big|^{1/6}=o(n^{-1/2}),$ as needed in (5), it implies that $\Big|\E\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(\mathsf{K}_{4,4})}(2\mathbf{G}_{i,j}-1)\Big|^{1/8}=o(n^{-3/16})$ which is too weak for our purposes.

We outline the scaling of Fourier coefficients to the power of $1/|\mathsf{V}(H)|$ as a second main challenge.

#### Challenge 2.

Developing techniques that not only compare Fourier coefficients, but do so with the appropriate $1/|\mathsf{V}(H)|$ scaling appearing in (5).

We note that this challenge is directly related to the one-to-one versus many-to-one comparisons discussed in Section 1.4.2 as apparent from the discussion above in Item 3.

Insight from Challenge 2: We need many-to-one comparison inequalities.

### 1.6 Our Key Ideas

We now describe our two main ideas used to overcome Challenge 1 and Challenge 2.

#### 1.6.1 Main Idea 1: Leaf-Isolation Technique

This idea is used to overcome both challenges and appears in the proofs of both part 3 and part 4 of Theorem 1.4. For simplicity, we illustrate with part 3. That is, $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ satisfies that each community label $i\in[k]$ appears with probability $p_{i}$ at least $c$ for some absolute constant $c>0$ (which implies that $k\leq 1/c=O(1).$ ) An elementary calculation (Lemma 3.2) shows that

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})=\Omega(\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|^{4}). $$

Hence, for any graph $H$ that satisfies $h=|\mathsf{V}(H)|\leq|\mathsf{E}(H)|,$ by (7)

$$ \begin{split}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|&=\Big|\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Big)\Big|\\
&\leq\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}|Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}|\Big)\\
&\lesssim\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|^{|\mathsf{E}(H)|}\leq\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\lesssim|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}},\end{split} $$

which is enough. Note that so far we have overcome Challenge 1 by directly comparing to a 4-cycle. What does remain a difficulty is Challenge 2. If we use (13) for a tree $T,$ the scaling is too weak as we obtain $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{E}(T)|}}\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{E}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}}$ and $|\mathsf{E}(T)|=|\mathsf{V}(T)|-1.$

*Figure 1: Illustration of the leaf-isolation inequality over the graph $H$ with leaves $5,6.$ It effectively compares $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|$ to $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H^{\prime}\sqcup\mathsf{Star}_{2})|=|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H^{\prime})|\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|.$ In this comparison, a new vertex $7$ is created, which resolves the issue that $|\mathsf{E}(H)|<|\mathsf{V}(H)|.$*

#### Leaf-Isolation Technique.

When $T$ is a tree on at least 3 vertices, $T$ has at least two leaves. Let these be $h-1,h$ with parents $\mathsf{par}(h-1),\mathsf{par}(h).$ Instead of the crude triangle inequality applied as a first step in (13), we use a more fine-grained “leaf-isolation” triangle inequality which allows us to artificially create a star count in (13) as in the figure. On a more technical level, we perform the summation over all vertices but the two leaves first and then over the two leaves:

$$ \begin{split}\Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)\Big|&=\Big|\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(T)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Big)\Big|\\
&=\Bigg|\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h-2}}\Bigg(p_{x_{1}}p_{x_{2}}\cdots p_{x_{h-2}}\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(T)\backslash\{(\mathsf{par}(h-1),h-1),(\mathsf{par}(h),h)\}}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\times\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\big(\sum_{x_{h-1}}p_{x_{h-1}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h-1)},x_{h-1}}\big)\times\big(\sum_{x_{h}}p_{x_{h}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h)}x_{h}}\big)\Bigg)\Bigg|\\
&\leq\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h-2}}\Bigg(p_{x_{1}}p_{x_{2}}\cdots p_{x_{h-2}}\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(T)\backslash\{(\mathsf{par}(h-1),h-1),(\mathsf{par}(h),h)\}}|Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}|\times\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\times\big|\sum_{x_{h-1}}p_{x_{h-1}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h-1)},x_{h-1}}\big|\times\big|\sum_{x_{h}}p_{x_{h}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h)},x_{h}}\big|\Bigg)\\
&\lesssim\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h-2}}\Bigg(\prod_{(ij)\in\mathsf{E}(T)\backslash\{(\mathsf{par}(h-1),h-1),(\mathsf{par}(h),h)\}}|Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}|\times\\
&\quad\quad\quad\quad\times\bigg(\big(\sum_{x_{h-1}}p_{x_{h-1}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h-1)},x_{h-1}}\big)^{2}+\big(\sum_{x_{h}}p_{x_{h}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h)},x_{h}}\big)^{2}\bigg)\Bigg),\end{split} $$

where we used $|a|\times|b|\leq a^{2}+b^{2}$ in the last line. Now, the product of $|\mathsf{E}(T)|-2=|\mathsf{V}(T)|-3$ values $Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}$ can be bounded as $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(T)|-3}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}},$ which is comparable to the signed count of a graph on $|\mathsf{V}(T)|-3$ vertices. On the other hand, $\big(\sum_{x_{h-1}}p_{x_{h-1}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h-1)},x_{h-1}}\big)^{2}+\big(\sum_{x_{h}}p_{x_{h}}Q_{x_{\mathsf{par}(h)}x_{h}}\big)^{2}$ can be easily shown to be bounded by $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2}),$ a graph on $3$ vertices. Altogether, we have managed to show that

$$ \Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)\Big|\lesssim|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(T)|-3}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}}\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|. $$

This immediately implies

$$ \Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)\Big|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(T)|}}\lesssim\max\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}}},|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|}}\Big). $$

#### 1.6.2 Main Idea 2: Comparison With a Non-Negative Model

The reason why the leaf-isolation technique alone is not sufficient for general SBMs on two communities is that (12) fails. Namely, one can show (Claim 3.4) that

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})=\Theta\bigg(\max\Big(p_{1}^{4}|Q_{1,1}|^{4},p^{2}_{1}p_{2}^{2}|Q_{1,2}|,p_{2}^{4}|Q_{2,2}|^{4}\Big)\bigg). $$

So, if $p_{1}$ is very small, say $p_{1}=n^{-1/2},$ then the inequality used in (13) for non-tree graphs may fail. Indeed, in Theorem A.8 we show that there do exist two-community SBMs and connected $H$ which are not trees such that $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=\omega(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})|}}).$

Thus, if we want to utilize (15) towards the leaf-isolation technique, we need to understand how the probability vector $(p_{1},p_{2})$ relates to the entries of $Q.$

#### Comparison with Non-Negative SBM.

To do so, we compare with a non-negative SBM and utilize what we know from [YZZ24] (spelled out in Section 1.5.1). Namely, let $|Q|$ be the matrix $Q$ in which we take entry-wise absolute values. Then, triangle inequality applied to (7) implies that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(H)|. $$

On the other hand, as explained in (1.5.1),

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|}} $$

for some $\mathbf{T}\in[1,|\mathsf{E}(H)|].$ Combining the last two inequalities, we conclude that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|}}. $$

Hence, the desired conclusion for 2-SBMs in Theorem 1.4 would be implied by

$$ \displaystyle|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|\lesssim|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})|\Longleftrightarrow \displaystyle p_{1}(p_{1}|Q_{1,1}|+p_{2}|Q_{1,2}|)^{\mathbf{T}}+p_{2}(p_{1}|Q_{1,2}|+p_{2}|Q_{2,2}|)^{\mathbf{T}}\lesssim\Big|p_{1}(p_{1}Q_{1,1}+p_{2}Q_{1,2})^{\mathbf{T}}+p_{2}(p_{1}Q_{1,2}+p_{2}Q_{2,2})^{\mathbf{T}}\Big|. $$

Unfortunately, such an inequality is wrong as demonstrated, for example, by Theorem A.2. Yet, whenever this inequality is violated, there must be certain cancellations in $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,|Q|)}(\mathsf{Star}_{\mathbf{T}})=p_{1}(p_{1}Q_{1,1}+p_{2}Q_{1,2})^{\mathbf{T}}+p_{2}(p_{1}Q_{1,2}+p_{2}Q_{2,2})^{\mathbf{T}}.$ The key question, used to address Challenge 1, is: What causes the cancellations? It turns out that the following dichotomy occurs. Exactly one of the following two types of cancellations occurs:

- 1. Within-community cancellations: when there is a cancellation within community 1, corresponding to $|p_{1}Q_{1,1}+p_{2}Q_{1,2}|=o(p_{1}|Q_{1,1}|+p_{2}|Q_{1,2}|)$ or, similarly in community 2, $|p_{1}Q_{1,2}+p_{2}Q_{2,2}|=o(p_{1}|Q_{1,2}|+p_{2}|Q_{2,2}|)$ .

- 2. Between-community cancellations: when there are no in-community cancellations, but there is a cancellation between $p_{1}(p_{1}Q_{1,1}+p_{2}Q_{1,2})^{\mathbf{T}}$ and $p_{2}(p_{1}Q_{1,2}+p_{2}Q_{2,2})^{\mathbf{T}}.$

In either case, the cancellations imply strong relationships between $Q$ and $p,$ which help us boost (15) and then apply an appropriate version of the leaf-isolation technique. For example, if $p_{1}\leq p_{2}$ (so, also $p_{2}\geq 1/2$ ) in the case of within-community cancellations we can show that $p_{2}|Q_{1,2}|=O(p_{1}|Q_{1,1}|),$ which turns out to be sufficient for making the leaf-isolation technique to work. The reason such an inequality is useful is the following. As $p_{2}\geq 1/2,$ it implies that $|Q_{1,2}|=O(p_{1}|Q_{1,1}|).$ This means that when applying the triangle-inequality approach (13) (or the more sophisticated leaf-isolation variation of it, (14)), we can replace some of the $Q_{1,2}$ occurrences with $p_{1}|Q_{1,1}|,$ thus, adding more $p_{1}$ appearances in the expression. As (15) reads $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})=\Theta\bigg(\max\Big(p_{1}^{4}|Q_{1,1}|^{4},p^{2}_{1}|Q_{1,2}|,|Q_{2,2}|^{4}\Big)\bigg)$ when $p_{2}\geq 1/2,$ the extra occurrences of $p_{1}$ are key to a comparison with $\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}).$

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Notation

#### Graph Notation.

All graphs in the current paper are undirected and have no loops or multiple edges. For a graph $H,$ its vertex set and edge sets are denoted by $\mathsf{V}(H)$ and $\mathsf{E}(H).$ Whenever $A,B\subseteq\mathsf{V}(H)$ for some graph $H,$ we denote by $\mathsf{E}_{H}(A,B)$ the subset of $\mathsf{E}(H)$ with one endpoint in $A$ and one endpoint in $B.$ For $S\subseteq\mathsf{V}(H),$ we denote by $H|_{S}$ the graph on vertex set $S$ and edge-set $\mathsf{E}_{H}(S,S).$

We denote by $\mathsf{Cyc}_{t}$ the cycle on $t$ vertices, by $\mathsf{K}_{t}$ the complete graph on $t$ vertices, by $\mathsf{K}_{t,s}$ the complete bipartite graph on parts with $t$ and $s$ vertices, by $\mathsf{Star}_{t}$ the star graph on $t+1$ vertices (so $\mathsf{K}_{1,t}=\mathsf{Star}_{t}$ ). In $\mathsf{Star}_{t},$ there is one central vertex of degree $t,$ which is adjacent to $t$ leaves. Note that $\mathsf{Star}_{1}$ is simply an edge and $\mathsf{Star}_{2}$ is the path of length 2 (also called wedge).

For two graphs $H,K,$ we denote by $H\sqcup K$ their disjoint union. If $H$ and $K$ are labeled, denote by $H\otimes K$ the graph in which $(i,j)$ is an edge if and only if it is an edge in exactly one of $H$ and $K,$ and furthemrore all isolated vertices are removed.

For two graphs $H$ and $K,$ we denote by $H\sim K$ the fact that they are isomorphic.

Denote by $\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}$ the set of graphs without isolated vertices and at most $D$ edges and by $\mathsf{CGraphs}_{\leq D}$ those of them that are furthermore connected.

#### Asymptotic Notation.

For two quantities $x(n),y(n)\in\mathbb{R}$ depending on $n\in\mathbb{N},$ we denote $x\gtrsim y$ if $x\geq Cy$ for some absolute constant $C>0.$ If $x\gtrsim y$ and $y\gtrsim x,$ we denote $x\asymp y.$ We similarly denote $x\gtrsim_{D}y$ if $x\geq C(D)y$ where the constant $C(D)$ can be an arbitrary function of $D$ (but nothing else) and likewise $x\asymp_{D}y$ . We also denote by $y=O(x)$ and $x=\Omega(y)$ the fact $x\gtrsim y.$ Finally, $y=o_{n}(x)$ and $x=\omega_{n}(y)$ denote the fact that $\lim_{n\longrightarrow+\infty}y/x=0.$ In most places, we omit the dependence on $n.$

### 2.2 Testing via Low Degree Polynomials

Condition (2) is a special case of testing between two distributions via low-degree polynomial tests. Since the indicator of edges of a random graph are random variables, one naturally defines low-degree polynomial tests as follows, again exploiting Chebyshov’s ineqality.

#### Definition 2 ([HS17a, Hop18] specialized to graphs).

Consider the families of graph distributions $(\mathbb{P}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}.$ We say that a polynomial $f:\{0,1\}^{\binom{n}{2}}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ distinguishes the two families of distributions if

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}f(\mathbf{G})-\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}f(\mathbf{G})\Big|=\omega\Bigg(\max\Big(\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2},\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}[f(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2}\Big)\Bigg). $$

Conversely, if a polynomial $f$ of degree at most $D$ satisfies

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}f(\mathbf{G})-\E_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}f(\mathbf{G})\Big|=o\Bigg(\max\Big(\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2},\var_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathbb{P}_{n}}[f(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2}\Big)\Bigg), $$

we say that $f$ fails to distinguish the two distributions. If all polynomials of degree at most $D$ fail, we say that ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ are degree- $D$ indistinguishable.

Polynomials tests of degree $D=O(\log n)$ capture a wide range of computationally efficient tests such as constant-sized (signed) subgraph counts, certain spectral methods [KWB19], statistical-query algorithms [BBH+21], and approximate message passing [MW22] algorithms among others. Due to the variety of methods captured by low-degree polynomials, hardness against degree $D$ polynomials for some $D=\omega(\log n)$ is viewed as a strong (but, of course, still limited) heuristic for the computational hardness of a problem [HS17b, Hop18].

When testing against ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)},$ it is convenient to express polynomials in terms of the Fourier characters $\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(2G_{ji}-1).$ The key simple fact from Boolean Fourier analysis is the following.

#### Theorem 2.1 (Folklore).

The set of polynomials $\Bigg\{\prod_{(ji)\in E(H)}(2G_{ji}-1)\Bigg\}_{H}$ where $H$ ranges over all graphs without isolated vertices in $\mathsf{K}_{n}$ forms an orthonormal basis of all edge-functions over $n$ -vertex graphs with respect to the ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ distribution.

### 2.3 Simple Facts about Fourier Coefficients of Stochastic Block Models

#### Proposition 2.2.

Consider any stochastic block model $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ and let $H,K$ be any two graphs. Then,

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H\sqcup K)=\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\times\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K). $$

#### Proof.

Since there are no shared vertices between the copies of $H,K$ in $H\sqcup K$ and labels are independent,

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H\sqcup K)=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H\cup K)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}}\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}}\times\prod_{(u,v)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{u}\mathbf{x}_{v}}\Bigg] \displaystyle=\E\Bigg[\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}}\Bigg]\times\E\Bigg[\prod_{(u,v)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{\mathbf{x}_{u}\mathbf{x}_{v}}\Bigg]=\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\times\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K).\qed $$

#### Corollary 2.1.

Consider any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ distribution and let $H,K$ be any two graphs. Then,

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H\sqcup K)\leq\max\Big(\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H),\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)\Big). $$

#### Proof.

Recalling the definition of $\Psi,$

$$ \displaystyle|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H\sqcup K)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H\sqcup K)|}} \displaystyle=\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)|\Big)^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|+|\mathsf{V}(H)|}} \displaystyle=\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\Big)^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|+|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\times\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}}\Big)^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|+|\mathsf{V}(H)|}} \displaystyle\leq\max\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}},|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}}\Big)^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|+|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\times \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\times\max\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}},|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}}\Big)^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|+|\mathsf{V}(H)|}} \displaystyle=\max\Big(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}},|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(K)|}}\Big).\qed $$

#### Corollary 2.2 (Star Counts).

For any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ model on $k$ communities

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{t})=\sum_{x\in[k]}p_{x}\times\big(\sum_{y\in[k]}Q_{x,y}p_{y}\big)^{t}. $$

#### Proof.

Follows from Proposition 1.3 by first summing over the central vertex. ∎

### 2.4 Meta Theorems on Signed Subgraph Counts

#### Theorem 2.3 (Beating Null Variance by A Low Degree Polynomial).

Suppose that $(\mathbb{P}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a family of vertex-symmetric distributions over $n$ -vertex graphs and there exists some polynomial $f$ of constant degree $D$ such that

$$ |\E_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[f]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f]|=\omega(\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f]^{1/2}). $$

Then, there exists some subgraph $H$ on at most $D$ vertices such that $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\omega(n^{-1/2}).$

#### Proof.

Recall that $\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}$ is the set of graphs without isolated vertices on at most $D$ edges. Consider the polynomial

$$ f(G)=\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2G_{ji}-1). $$

Then, by orthonormality under the ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ distribution (Theorem 2.1),

$$ \displaystyle\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f(\mathbf{G})]=\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c^{2}_{H_{1}}. $$

Hence, as $D$ is constant and there are constantly many graphs without isolated vertices and at most $D$ edges, it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f(\mathbf{G})]^{1/2} \displaystyle=\Bigg(\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c^{2}_{H_{1}}\Bigg)^{1/2} \displaystyle=\Theta\Bigg(\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\Big(\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c^{2}_{H_{1}}\Big)^{1/2}\Bigg). $$

At the same time,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[f]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f]\Big| \displaystyle=\Big|\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}\E_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Big| \displaystyle=\Big|\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\Big| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\Big|\times\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}|c_{H_{1}}| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\Big|\times\frac{\Big({\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}^{2}}\Big)^{1/2}}{\Big({\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}1}\Big)^{1/2}}\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad(\text{Cauchy-Schwartz}) \displaystyle=\Theta\Bigg(\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)\Big|\times\frac{\Big({\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}^{2}}\Big)^{1/2}}{n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2}}\Bigg). $$

Hence, $|\E_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}[f]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f]|=\omega(\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[f]^{1/2})$ implies that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}|\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)|\times\frac{\Big({\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}^{2}}\Big)^{1/2}}{n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2}}=\omega\Bigg(\sum_{H\in\mathsf{Graphs}_{\leq D}}\Big(\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c^{2}_{H_{1}}\Big)^{1/2}\Bigg). $$

As the sum is over constantly many terms, at most $2^{O(D\log D)}$ (which is an upper bound on the number of graphs without isolated vertices and at most $D$ edges), there exists some $H$ such that $\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}^{2}\neq 0$ and

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{P}_{n}}(H)|\times\frac{\Big({\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c_{H_{1}}^{2}}\Big)^{1/2}}{n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2}}=\omega\Bigg(\Big(\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H\sim H_{1}}c^{2}_{H_{1}}\Big)^{1/2}\Bigg). $$

the claim follows.∎

Recall that the reason (5) is not sufficient to conclude that a given signed subgraph count is a good tester is that (5) does not take into account the variance under the planted distribution. Somewhat surprisingly, it turns out that the variance of the planted model is actually captured by this equation by the maximizer of $K\longrightarrow\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}}(K).$

#### Theorem 2.4 (Beating Variance of Null Implies Beating Variance of Planted).

Suppose that $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ is any SBM model and let $D$ be any constant (independent of $n$ ). Suppose that the connected graph $H$ on at most $D$ vertices satisfies the following two properties:

- 1. $\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\omega(n^{-1/2}).$

- 2. $H$ is an approximate maximizer of $K\longrightarrow\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)$ in the following sense.

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\gtrsim_{D}\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(K)\text{ for any }K\text{on at most $2D$ edges.} $$

Then, one can test between $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ and ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ using the signed $H$ count, namely

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]\Big|=\omega\Big(\max(\var_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]^{1/2},\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]^{1/2})\Big). $$

#### Proof.

Due to the $\Theta(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|})$ isomorphic copies of $H,$

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]\Big|=\Theta(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|). $$

Hence, $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=\omega(n^{-1/2})$ immediately implies that

$$ \Big|\E_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]\Big|=\omega(n^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|/2})=\omega(\var_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]^{1/2}). $$

Thus, all we need to show is that

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\E_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]\Big|=\omega(\var_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]^{1/2}). $$

For the left hand-side, we use (19). The right hand-side we expand as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\var_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}] \displaystyle=\var_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}\Bigg[\sum_{H_{1}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H}\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg] \displaystyle=\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H}{\rm Cov}_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1),\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]. $$

Note that if $H_{1},H_{2}$ don’t have a common vertex, the covariance is clearly zero. Hence, the above expression equals

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}{\rm Cov}_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1),\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg] \displaystyle=\sum\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\Bigg|\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg] \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad-\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]\Bigg| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\Bigg(\Bigg|\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]\Bigg| \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]^{2}\Bigg) \displaystyle=\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\Bigg(\Bigg|\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})\triangle\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]\Bigg| \displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad+\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]^{2}\Bigg). $$

First, we will bound the term

$$ \sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]^{2}. $$

Note that there are $O(n^{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|-1})$ terms in the sum. This is the case since $|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cup\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|\leq 2|\mathsf{V}(H)|-1$ whenever $\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset.$ Furthermore, each of these terms is $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{2}.$ Altogether,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]^{2} \displaystyle=O\Big(n^{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|-1}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{2}\Big)=o\Big(\Big|\E_{\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]-\E_{{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}}[\mathsf{SC}_{H}]\Big|^{2}\Big) $$

by (19). Next, consider

$$ \sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\Bigg|\E\Bigg[\prod_{(ji)\in\mathsf{E}(H_{1})\triangle\mathsf{E}(H_{2})}(2\mathbf{G}_{ji}-1)\Bigg]\Bigg|. $$

Note that the graph defined by edges $\mathsf{E}(H_{1})\triangle\mathsf{E}(H_{2})$ is exactly $H_{1}\otimes H_{2}.$ Hence, the above sum is

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{H_{1},H_{2}\subseteq K_{n}\;:\;H_{1}\sim H,H_{2}\sim H,\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\neq\emptyset}\big|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})\big|. $$

Denote the following cardinalities:

$$ \begin{split}&s_{\emptyset}=|(\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cup\mathsf{V}(H_{2}))\backslash\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|,\\
&s_{1}=|(\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2}))\backslash\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|,\\
&s_{2}=|(\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2}))\backslash\mathsf{V}(H_{1})|,\\
&s_{1,2}=|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{2})\cap\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|\end{split} $$

A simple count shows that

$$ \begin{split}&s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}=|\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|,\\
&s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{1,2}=|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})|=|\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|=s_{\emptyset}+s_{2}+s_{1,2},\\
&s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}=|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cup\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|.\end{split} $$

The number of ways to choose $H_{1},H_{2}\sim H$ so that $|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})\cup\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|=s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}$ is $O(n^{s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}).$ Hence, the number of terms in (20) with the specific overlap pattern of $H_{1},H_{2}$ satisfying (21) is $O(n^{s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}).$ As there are constantly many choices of $s_{\emptyset},s_{1},s_{2},s_{1,2}$ (as $H_{1},H_{2}$ are two graphs on constantly many vertices), recalling (19), it is enough to show that for any choice for $s_{\emptyset},s_{1},s_{2},s_{1,2},$

$$ \displaystyle n^{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{2}=\omega\Bigg(n^{s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|\Bigg). $$

Using the fact that $|\mathsf{E}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|=|\mathsf{E}(H_{1})\triangle\mathsf{E}(H_{2})|\leq|\mathsf{E}(H_{1})|+|\mathsf{E}(H_{2})|\leq 2D$ by condition 2., the approximate optimality of $H,$ it follows that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|}}=O(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}). $$

Hence, it is enough to show that

$$ \displaystyle n^{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{2}=\omega\Bigg(n^{s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{|\mathsf{V}(H_{1}\otimes H_{2})|}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\Bigg). $$

Recalling (22) and the fact that $|\mathsf{V}(H)|=\frac{1}{2}(|\mathsf{V}(H_{1})|+|\mathsf{V}(H_{2})|),$ we need to show that

$$ \displaystyle n^{s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2}}\times|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{2}=\omega\Bigg(n^{s_{\emptyset}+s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2}}{(s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2})/2}}\Bigg)\quad\Longleftrightarrow \displaystyle|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{2(s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2})-2(s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{1,2})}{s_{1}+s_{2}+2s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2}}}=\omega(n^{-s_{\emptyset}-s_{1,2}})\quad\Longleftrightarrow \displaystyle|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{4s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2}}{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=\omega(n^{-s_{\emptyset}-s_{1,2}}). $$

This last inequality follows from condition 1. that $|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=\omega(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}).$ Concretely,

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{4s_{\emptyset}+2s_{1,2}}{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\geq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{4s_{\emptyset}+4s_{1,2}}{2|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}=\Bigg(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\Bigg)^{2(s_{\emptyset}+s_{1,2})}=\omega(n^{-s_{\emptyset}-s_{1,2}}). $$

Thus, we have shown (23) for one possible choice of $s_{\emptyset},s_{1},s_{2},s_{1,2}$ in (21). Enumerating over the constantly many possible choices for $s_{\emptyset},s_{1},s_{2},s_{1,2}$ gives the result. ∎

## 3 Proofs of Main Results

### 3.1 Diagonal SBMs

In this section, we study the family of $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ models where all off-diagonal entries of $Q$ are non-zero. This is equivalent to saying that whenever two vertices have distinct labels, the probability they are adjacent is exactly $1/2.$

#### Theorem 3.1 (Maximizing Partition Functions in Diagonal SBMs).

Suppose that $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ is such that $Q$ is diagonal. Then, for any connected graph $H,$

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\max(\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{1}),\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})). $$

#### Proof.

Take any connected $H.$ Recall Proposition 1.3 stating that

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg). $$

Observe that since $Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}=0$ whenever $x_{i}\neq x_{j},$ the expression becomes

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times(Q_{x,x})^{|\mathsf{E}(H)|}. $$

In particular, for any graph $H,$ it is clearly the case that

$$ \begin{split}|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|&=\Big|\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times(Q_{x,x})^{|\mathsf{E}(H)|}\Big|\\
&\leq\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times|Q_{x,x}|^{|\mathsf{E}(H)|}\\
&\leq\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}\times|Q_{x,x}|^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|-1},\end{split} $$

where in the last line we used the fact that any connected graph on $v$ vertices has at least $v-1$ edges. Now, to finish the proof, we will use the fact that

$$ \displaystyle v\longrightarrow(\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{v}\times|Q_{x,x}|^{v-1})^{1/v} $$

is decreasing on $[1,+\infty)$ . This is a simple analytic inequality which we prove in Section B.1.

(25) implies that for any graph on at least three vertices (and there exists a unique connected graph on two vertices, $\mathsf{Star}_{1}$ ), it is the case that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\leq(\sum_{x\in[k]}(p_{x})^{3}\times|Q_{x,x}|^{2})^{\frac{1}{3}}=|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})|}}.\qed $$

Combining with Theorem 2.4, we obtain a result for the optimal constant degree distinguisher.

#### Theorem 3.2 (Testing in Diagonal SBMs).

Suppose that $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ is a stochastic block model with a diagonal matrix $Q.$ Then, if there exists a constant degree test distinguishing ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ with high probability, one can also distinguish the two distributions with high probability using the signed $\mathsf{Star}_{1}$ (edge) or $\mathsf{Star}_{2}$ (wedge) count.

### 3.2 Non-Negative SBMs

The case of non-negative SBMs is covered by [YZZ24]. Let us explain how to relate a non-negative SBM and the more general Theorem 1.2 of [YZZ24]. This relation also appears in the “planted dense subgraph application” of the main result of [YZZ24]. Namely, let $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ be a non-negative SBM. That, is $Q_{i,j}\geq 0\quad\forall i,j.$ Then, the probability of an edge between vertices with labels $i$ and $j$ is $(Q_{i,j}+1)/2=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{Q_{i,j}}{2}.$ The following procedure generates a sample from $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q):$

- 1. First, draw $n$ iid labels $\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}p.$

- 2. Then, draw a graph $H^{\prime}$ on vertex set $[n]$ by drawing an edge between $i,j$ with probability $Q_{\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}}.$

- 3. Let $H^{\prime}$ be a uniformly random vertex permutation of $H.$

- 4. Now, draw $\mathbf{K}\sim{\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and output $\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{K}\cup H.$

Step 4 shows that the model can be captured via the planted subgraph result of Theorem 1.2. We obtain the following corollary, implicit in [YZZ24].

#### Corollary 3.1 (Implicit in [YZZ24]).

Let $Q$ be a non-negative matrix. If there exists a degree- $D$ test distinguishing ${\mathbb{G}(n,1/2)}$ and $\mathbb{SBM}(n;p,Q)$ with high probability for some absolute constant $D,$ then one can also distinguish the two distribution with high probability using the signed count of some star on at most $D$ edges.

We still describe the corresponding partition function maximization step as it will be useful in the proof of Theorem 3.6 (our result for 2-SBMs).

#### Theorem 3.3 (Maximizing Partition Functions in Non-Negative SBMs).

Consider any $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ model in which all entries of the matrix $Q$ are non-negative. Then, for any connected graph $H$ on at most $D$ edges,

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\leq\max_{1\leq t\leq D}\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{t}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $H$ be any connected graph on at most $D$ edges. Again, we start by recalling Proposition 1.3:

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg). $$

Now, we make the following observation. Suppose that $H$ is not a tree. Then, one can remove some edge $(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)$ to obtain a graph $H^{\prime}$ that is still connected. Clearly,

$$ \begin{split}&\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H^{\prime})=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H^{\prime})}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg)\\
&\geq\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg)=\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H),\end{split} $$

where we used the simple fact that $Q\in[0,1]$ and $\mathsf{E}(H^{\prime})\subseteq\mathsf{E}(H).$

Repeating the same edge-removal procedure, we are left with some spanning tree $T$ of $H$ such that

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)\geq\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H). $$

As $T$ is spanning, $|\mathsf{V}(T)|=|\mathsf{V}(H)|,$ so

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(T)|}}\geq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}. $$

Now, we will further remove edges from the tree. Suppose that $T$ is not a star. Then, it has a subgraph which is a path of length 3. Removing the middle edge partitions $T$ into two trees (both with at least one edge) such that $\mathsf{V}(T_{1})\cup\mathsf{V}(T_{2})=\mathsf{V}(T)$ and $\mathsf{V}(T_{1})\cap\mathsf{V}(T_{2})=\emptyset.$ Using the same-argument as in (26), we conclude that

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T_{1}\sqcup T_{2})\geq\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T). $$

Using Corollary 2.1, we conclude that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(T)|}}\leq\max(|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T_{1})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(T_{1})|}},|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(T_{2})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(T_{2})|}}). $$

Repeating this operation while no paths of length at least 3 are left, we conclude that

$$ |\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}}\leq|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{t})|^{\frac{1}{|\mathsf{V}(\mathsf{Star}_{t})|}} $$

for some star graph on $t\leq D$ edges. ∎

### 3.3 SBMs with Non-Vanishing Community Probabilities

#### Theorem 3.4 (Maximizing Partition Functions with Non-Vanishing Community Probabilities).

Suppose that $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ is a stochastic block model on $k$ communities such that $p_{i}\geq c\;\forall i\in[k]$ for some constant $c>0.$ Then, for any connected graph $H$ on at most $D$ edges,

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\lesssim_{c,D}\max\bigg(\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}),\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{1}),\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Star}_{2})\bigg). $$

#### Proof.

Denote $h=|\mathsf{V}(H)|.$ We split the proof into two parts depending on whether $H$ is a tree.

#### 1. $H$ is not a tree.

In that case, we can show that 4-cycles “dominate” $H.$ We need the following statement on signed 4-cycle counts.

#### Lemma 3.2.

Suppose that $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ is a stochastic block model on $k$ communities such that $p_{i}\geq c\;\forall i\in[k]$ for some universal constant $c>0.$ Then,

$$ \Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})\gtrsim_{c}\max_{i,j\in[k]}Q^{4}_{i,j}\text{ and, equivalently, }\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4})\gtrsim_{c}\max_{i,j\in[k]}|Q_{i,j}|. $$

Before we present the proof of the lemma, we will show that it immediately implies the following statement.

#### Claim 3.3.

Under the assumptions on $\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)$ in Theorem 3.4, for any connected graph $H$ which is not a tree,

$$ \Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\lesssim_{c,D}\Psi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}). $$

#### Proof.

Since $H$ is not a tree, $|\mathsf{V}(H)|\leq|\mathsf{E}(H)|.$ Recalling Proposition 1.3,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(H)\Big|=\Bigg|\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\Bigg(\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}Q_{x_{i},x_{j}}\Bigg)\Bigg| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}\times\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathsf{E}(H)}(\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|) \displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}(\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|)^{|\mathsf{E}(H)|} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{h}\in[k]}\prod_{i=1}^{h}p_{x_{i}}(\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|)^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|} \displaystyle=(\max_{u,v}|Q_{u,v}|)^{|\mathsf{V}(H)|}. $$

The claim follows immediately from Lemma 3.2. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 3.2.

We start by analyzing Proposition 1.3:

$$ \displaystyle\Phi_{\mathbb{SBM}(p,Q)}(\mathsf{Cyc}_{4}) \displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}}p_{x_{1}}p_{x_{2}}p_{x_{3}}p_{x_{4}}Q_{x_{1},x_{2}}Q_{x_{2},x_{3}}Q_{x_{3},x_{4}}Q_{x_{4},x_{1}} \displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1},x_{3}}p_{x_{1}}p_{x_{3}}\Bigg(\sum_{x}p_{x}Q_{x_{1},x}Q_{x,x_{3}}\Bigg)^{2} \displaystyle\geq\sum_{y}p_{y}^{2}\Bigg(\sum_{x}p_{x}Q_{y,x}Q_{y,x}\Bigg)^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{y}p_{y}^{2}\Bigg(\sum_{x}p_{x}Q_{y,x}^{2}\Bigg)^{2} \displaystyle\geq\sum_{y}p_{y}^{2}\sum_{x}p_{x}^{2}Q_{x,y}^{4}=\sum_{x,y}p_{x}^{2}p_{y}^{2}Q_{x,y}^{4}\geq\max_{x,y}c^{4}Q_{x,y}^{4}\gtrsim_{c}\max_{x,y}Q_{x,y}^{4}, $$

as desired. ∎

#### 2. $H$ is a tree.

Suppose that $H$ is a tree. We can assume that $H$ has at least three edges as otherwise $H$ is a star and there is nothing to prove. In particular, this means that $H$ has at least two leaves.
